```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
library(SMSD)
# Three decimal places for numbers written into the text.
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
```

## The Applied Scenario

A management researcher at a regional bank is studying whether a new
onboarding program improves the engagement of new hires six months after
their start date. Two cohorts are recruited: one assigned to the new
program ("treatment") and one that continues with the existing program
("control"). Engagement is measured on a scale from 1 to 7.

The effect size of interest is the standardized mean difference, &delta;
= (&mu;<sub>1</sub> &minus; &mu;<sub>2</sub>) / &sigma;: the difference
between the two population means in units of the common standard
deviation. The researcher wants to report how large the effect of the
program is, with a confidence interval narrow enough to be useful, which
is the accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) approach to study design
(Maxwell, Kelley, & Rausch, 2008).

A fixed sample size plan for that goal (Kelley & Rausch, 2006;
`DMAR::ss_aipe_smd()`) needs a planning value for &delta;, which is the
quantity the study is being run to estimate. The sequential AIPE
procedure of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018) needs none. Data
are collected in stages, and sampling stops at the first stage at which
the stopping rule says the confidence interval is narrow enough. The
procedure is distribution free: it does not assume that engagement
scores are normal.

## The Plan

Before any data are collected the researcher fixes three things and
writes them down: the target full width of the confidence interval (the
upper limit minus the lower limit, which the article calls omega), the
confidence level, and how often the stopping rule will be checked.
Here the target width is 0.30 at 95% confidence, and the rule will be
checked after every 10 new hires per cohort.

```{r plan}
target_width <- 0.30
conf_level <- 0.95
batch_size <- 10

m <- seq_aipe_smd_pilot(width = target_width, conf_level = conf_level)
m
```

The first stage collects `r m` new hires per cohort. The pilot sample
size is the larger of a minimum (`m_0`, 4 by default, the fewest
observations from which the variance estimate can be computed) and
twice the standard normal quantile for the confidence level, divided by
the target width and rounded up (Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2018,
Equation 21):

```{r plan-pilot}
ceiling(2 * qnorm(1 - (1 - conf_level) / 2) / target_width)
```

## Stage 1: The Pilot

So that the vignette can be run, the data are simulated from a known
population; in a real study each call below is a new group of
participants. The program raises mean engagement from 4.5 to 4.8, and
the standard deviation is 0.9 in both cohorts, so the population
standardized mean difference is 0.3 / 0.9 = 0.33.

```{r pilot}
set.seed(113)
new_treatment <- function(n) rnorm(n, mean = 4.8, sd = 0.9)
new_control <- function(n) rnorm(n, mean = 4.5, sd = 0.9)

treatment <- new_treatment(m)
control <- new_control(m)

out <- seq_aipe_smd(group_1 = treatment, group_2 = control,
                    width = target_width, conf_level = conf_level)
out
attr(out, "is_satisfied")
```

```{r pilot-values, include = FALSE}
pilot_check <- summary(out)
```

The rule is not met. With `r pilot_check$current_n` per cohort the
interval is `r round(pilot_check$upper_limit - pilot_check$lower_limit, 2)`
wide, and the criterion sample size, the per cohort sample size the rule
currently asks for, is `r pilot_check$criterion_n`. The criterion is
computed from the variance estimate in the row `xi_squared`, so it is an
estimate too, and it will move as the data accumulate. The researcher
does not collect `r pilot_check$criterion_n` per cohort and stop; the
researcher keeps collecting and checking.

## Stages 2 and Beyond: The Loop

This loop is the study. Each pass recruits one more batch per cohort and
calls `seq_aipe_smd()` on all of the data collected so far. The cap on
the number of stages stands in for whatever practical limit a real
study has; if the cap ended the loop, the rule would not have been met,
and the width of the interval would not be guaranteed.

```{r loop}
max_stages <- 60

for (stage in seq_len(max_stages)) {
  treatment <- c(treatment, new_treatment(batch_size))
  control <- c(control, new_control(batch_size))

  out <- seq_aipe_smd(group_1 = treatment, group_2 = control,
                      width = target_width, conf_level = conf_level)

  if (attr(out, "is_satisfied")) break
}

stage
out
```

```{r loop-values, include = FALSE}
final <- summary(out)
final_width <- final$upper_limit - final$lower_limit
covers <- final$lower_limit <= 0.3 / 0.9 && 0.3 / 0.9 <= final$upper_limit
```

The rule was met after `r stage` batches, at `r final$current_n` new
hires per cohort. The estimate is `r f3(final$estimate)` with a 95%
confidence interval from `r f3(final$lower_limit)` to
`r f3(final$upper_limit)`. Its width, `r f3(final_width)`, is within
the target of 0.30, as it must be once the rule is met, and the
interval `r if (covers) "contains" else "does not contain"` the
population value of 0.33 from which the data were simulated.

## The Same Path in One Call

When the data are already in hand, `seq_path()` does what the loop did:
it applies the check function at each successive sample size and
returns every stage. All of the data go in its second argument, in the
order in which they were collected. With `by = batch_size` it checks at
the same stages as the study, starting from the pilot sample size.

```{r path}
path <- seq_path(seq_aipe_smd,
                 list(group_1 = treatment, group_2 = control),
                 width = target_width, conf_level = conf_level,
                 by = batch_size)
path
```

The stopping point is the one the loop found. The `plot()` method shows
the interval narrowing toward its target and the sample size reaching
the criterion.

```{r path-plot, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Two panels. Top: the estimated standardized mean difference with its confidence interval against the sample size per cohort; the interval narrows steadily and the stopping point is marked. Bottom: the current sample size rising to meet the criterion sample size, which stays near 345 after the first few stages."}
plot(path)
```

A path also answers a question the loop cannot: what did checking only
after every 10 new hires cost? With the default `by = 1` the rule is
evaluated after every new hire per cohort.

```{r path-one}
path_one <- seq_path(seq_aipe_smd,
                     list(group_1 = treatment, group_2 = control),
                     width = target_width, conf_level = conf_level)
attr(path_one, "stop_n")
```

Checked after every observation, the rule would first have been met at
`r attr(path_one, "stop_n")` per cohort; checked after every batch it
was met at `r attr(path, "stop_n")`. Checking in batches cost this
study `r attr(path, "stop_n") - attr(path_one, "stop_n")` new hires per
cohort, and its interval is a little narrower for them. (In simulations
reported in `?seq_aipe_sensitivity`, checking after every batch cost
about half a batch per group on average.) That comparison is a
description of this study after the fact. It is not a way to choose a
stopping point: the estimate to report is the one at the stage where
the study, run as planned, stopped. `?seq_path` explains why a later or
more favorable stage may not be substituted.

## Reporting

`seq_report()` turns a check or a path into the paragraph a methods
section needs, with the reference.

```{r report}
seq_report(path)
```

The paragraph says what a reader needs to evaluate the result:
the procedure, the target width and confidence level, where checking
began and how often the rule was checked, the sample size at which it
was met, and the estimate with its interval. Naming the procedure
matters because the final sample size was determined by the data, and
the properties of the interval are those of the interval at the
stopping point of this rule.

Those properties are of two kinds. The width is at most the target
whenever the rule is met; that holds in every sample. The coverage
approaches the confidence level as the target width narrows and the
final sample grows (Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2018, Theorem 2;
Theorem 4 states it for the standardized mean difference), and the
final sample size approaches the one a fixed sample size plan would
have used had the population values been known (their Lemma 3). For a
standardized mean difference of moderate size the approximation is good
at targets like this one: in simulations of the procedure as shipped,
95% intervals
contained a population value of 0.5 in 0.952 of studies at a target
width of 0.4 and in 0.946 at a width of 0.2 for normal data, and in
0.944 and 0.949 for right skewed data (6,000 and 2,000 studies; see
`?seq_aipe_smd`). To see what to expect for a particular design before
collecting data, use `seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity()`, described in
`vignette("sensitivity-analysis", package = "SMSD")`.

## Comparison With a Fixed Sample Size Plan

Had the researcher known that the population standardized mean
difference was 0.33, a fixed sample size plan for the same target would
have been available from DMAR. `ss_aipe_smd()` takes the planning value
`delta`, the confidence level, and the width; it has no argument for
the standard deviation, because &delta; is already in standard deviation
units.

```{r fixed}
fixed <- DMAR::ss_aipe_smd(delta = 0.3 / 0.9, conf_level = conf_level,
                           width = target_width)
print(fixed)
```

```{r fixed-values, include = FALSE}
n_fixed <- fixed$value[fixed$term == "necessary_n_per_group"]
```

The fixed plan asks for `r n_fixed` per cohort. The sequential study,
which was told nothing about &delta;, stopped at `r final$current_n`
(and would have stopped at `r attr(path_one, "stop_n")` had it checked
after every observation). The difference between the two approaches is
not the sample size they reach when the planning value is right. It is
what happens when the planning value is wrong:

```{r fixed-planning}
planning_values <- c(0, 0.3 / 0.9, 0.8)
n_planned <- sapply(planning_values, function(delta) {
  plan <- DMAR::ss_aipe_smd(delta = delta, conf_level = conf_level,
                            width = target_width)
  plan$value[plan$term == "necessary_n_per_group"]
})
data.frame(planning_value = round(planning_values, 2),
           n_per_cohort = n_planned)
```

A researcher who planned for no effect when the population value was
0.8 would have collected `r n_planned[1]` per cohort where
`r n_planned[3]` were needed, and the interval would be expected to come
out wider than 0.30. The sequential study has no planning value to get
wrong. For the standardized mean difference the required sample size
depends only mildly on &delta;, so the penalty is small. It is larger
for effect sizes whose sampling variance depends strongly on the
population value. For a correlation at a target width of 0.20, for
example, the fixed plan changes by more than a hundred pairs between
planning values of 0.1 and 0.5:

```{r fixed-r}
sapply(c(0.1, 0.5), function(rho) {
  plan <- DMAR::ss_aipe_r(rho = rho, width = 0.20, conf_level = conf_level)
  plan$value[plan$term == "necessary_N"]
})
```

What a sequential design asks in return is attention to the target
width and the pilot sample size, because its coverage guarantee is
asymptotic; `vignette("seq-aipe-correlations", package = "SMSD")` takes
that up for the correlation.

## Practical Questions

**What if the cohorts become unequal?** The stopping rule is stated for
the same number of observations in each group, and `seq_aipe_smd()`
stops with an error when the two groups differ in size (`seq_aipe_c()`
does the same for the groups of a contrast). A study that loses a
participant from one cohort recruits until the cohorts are level again.
Until they are, the rule can be checked on the first *n* observations of
each cohort in the order in which they were collected, where *n* is the
size of the smaller cohort. Which observations wait is settled by their
order and never by their values.

**What if the study has a limit it cannot pass?** Write the limit into
the plan, as the loop above does with its cap on the number of stages.
If the limit ends the study before the rule is met,
`attr(out, "is_satisfied")` is `FALSE`, the width of the interval is not
guaranteed, and the report says that sampling ended at the limit and not
by the rule. `seq_report()` describes a check whose rule is not met as a
study still under way, so that sentence of its paragraph is rewritten by
hand. A design with a limit can be studied in advance: the
`seq_aipe_*_sensitivity()` functions take the limit as `max_n`, and the
row `pct_hit_max_n` of their summary is the percentage of simulated
studies that the limit ended.

**What may be done with the data afterward?** The result of the
procedure is the estimate and the interval at the stage where the study,
run as planned, stopped, and the width and the coverage discussed above
belong to that interval. Other analyses of the same data, such as
another effect size or a significance test, are ordinary secondary
analyses of a sample whose size the data determined: nothing in the
procedure gives their intervals a width, and a report of them says how
the sample size was arrived at. Collecting more observations and
estimating again is a different procedure from the one planned, as is
choosing among the stages of a path.

## Connections to the Rest of SMSD

Every sequential procedure in the package has a pilot function, a check
function called after each stage, and `seq_report()` for the write-up.
`seq_path()` replays data in hand for the purely sequential procedures,
in which every group grows by the same number of observations at each
stage (for `seq_aipe_R2()` the pilot sample size is supplied as `start`,
because it depends on the number of predictors). It does not apply to
the two stage procedures, which have no stage by stage path, or to the
two designs whose groups grow at different rates: `seq_mr_smd()` with
two costs, and the budget procedure, whose loop is written with
`seq_budget_next()`.

- **Correlation coefficients:** `seq_aipe_r()` for a Pearson, Kendall,
  or Spearman correlation, and `seq_aipe_R2()` for the squared multiple
  correlation (Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2019). Example: how
  strongly time on task relates to a usability score. See
  `vignette("seq-aipe-correlations", package = "SMSD")`, which also
  explains why these procedures need narrower targets than the
  standardized mean difference does.
- **Coefficient of variation:** `seq_aipe_cv()` for the relative
  variability of a positive quantity, for example hospital length of
  stay.
- **Regression slope:** `seq_aipe_reg_coef()` for the slope of a simple
  linear regression, for example hours of tutoring predicting a test
  score.
- **Standardized mean:** `seq_aipe_sm()` for a mean in standard
  deviation units, for example a standardized mean change from pretest
  to posttest.
- **Contrast:** `seq_aipe_c()` for a contrast among the means of two or
  more groups, for example one condition against the average of two
  others.
- **Gini index:** `seq_aipe_gini()` for the inequality of incomes or
  sales (Chattopadhyay & De, 2016).
- **Minimum risk:** `seq_mr_smd()` and `seq_mr_cv()` stop when the cost
  of sampling plus the cost of estimation error is smallest, for studies
  in which each observation has a price (Chattopadhyay & Kelley, 2016,
  2017). See `vignette("mrpe-smd", package = "SMSD")` and
  `vignette("mrpe-cv", package = "SMSD")`.
- **A budget across groups:** `seq_budget()` with `seq_budget_next()`
  estimates a contrast among K groups as precisely as a fixed budget
  allows when the groups cost different amounts to sample, for example
  training formats with different costs per trainee (Chattopadhyay,
  Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, & Padalunkal, 2025). See
  `vignette("seq-budget", package = "SMSD")`.
